title: Brute force, credential stuffing and rate limits
summary: A login that answers ten thousand guesses a minute will be guessed. Tell brute force from credential stuffing, choose limits that do not lock out real users, and add ASP.NET Core's rate limiter with a 429 and Retry-After.

steps.title: Three ways in through the front door
body: - **Brute force / password guessing**: one account, many passwords. Stopped by per-account and per-address limits.
- **Password spraying**: one common password (`Winter2026!`), many accounts, slowly, so no single account trips a limit.

- **Credential stuffing**: username/password pairs leaked from *other* sites, tried here from thousands of IP addresses. Each pair is tried once, so per-account limits barely help; breached-password checks, MFA and bot detection do.
These are **A07:2025 Authentication Failures** (and API2:2023). Tools like hydra make them a one-liner, which is why the lab's task 17 takes seconds.

steps.prompt: Match each attack to the defence that hurts it most.
pairs: a per-account failure limit with growing delays
Leaked pairs from thousands of IPs

steps.title: Limits that do not lock out your users
body: A hard lockout ("10 failures and the account is locked for a day") is itself an attack: anyone can lock out the CEO by typing wrong passwords. Prefer:
- **Rate limits per address** (5 a minute, then `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After`), and **per account** with growing delays (1 s, 2 s, 4 s...) instead of a lock.
- **Same answer** for "no such user" and "wrong password", in the same time, so the login does not reveal who has an account (account enumeration; also check the sign-up and password-reset forms).
- **Breached-password checks** (NIST SP 800-63B): refuse passwords that appear in known breaches, instead of composition rules like "one digit, one symbol".

Behind a proxy or load balancer every request comes from the proxy's address. Configure `UseForwardedHeaders` with `KnownProxies`/`KnownNetworks` first, or the limit is shared by every user. And never trust `X-Forwarded-For` from the internet directly: an attacker sets a new one per request.

steps.prompt: The login is rate limited per IP from `X-Forwarded-For`, read straight from the request. There is no proxy in front of the app. What happens?
options: An attacker sends a different X-Forwarded-For with each request and is never limited
The limit works: X-Forwarded-For is set by the browser
Requests without the header are refused
steps.explain: Forwarded headers are only meaningful when your own proxy sets them and the app trusts only that proxy. Here it is attacker input.

steps.title: Rate limit the login
prompt: Add ASP.NET Core's built-in rate limiter (`using System.Threading.RateLimiting;`):
- a policy `login`: a **fixed window** of **5 requests per minute** per client address (`ctx.Connection.RemoteIpAddress`), no queue;
- rejected requests get `429` and a `Retry-After: 60` header (`o.OnRejected`);
**Run checks** sends six quick sign-ins from the same address.
starter: l.Username == "carol" && l.Password == "correct horse battery staple" ? Results.Ok(new { ok = true }) : Results.Unauthorized());
solution: _ => new FixedWindowRateLimiterOptions { PermitLimit = 5, Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1), QueueLimit = 0 }));
l.Username == "carol" && l.Password == "correct horse battery staple" ? Results.Ok(new { ok = true }) : Results.Unauthorized())
hints: Inside: `o.RejectionStatusCode = 429; o.AddPolicy("login", ctx => RateLimitPartition.GetFixedWindowLimiter(ctx.Connection.RemoteIpAddress?.ToString() ?? "unknown", _ => new FixedWindowRateLimiterOptions { PermitLimit = 5, Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1), QueueLimit = 0 }));`
template: public static async Task Run(HttpClient http)
await Dojo.TryAsync("The login could be called", async () =>
DojoWeb.Status("the right password works", 200, await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/login", new { username = "carol", password = "correct horse battery staple" }));
DojoWeb.Status($"wrong guess {i} is a normal 401", 401, await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/login", new { username = "carol", password = $"guess{i}" }));
var limited = await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/login", new { username = "carol", password = "correct horse battery staple" });
DojoWeb.Status("the 6th request in a minute gets 429, even with the right password", 429, limited);
Dojo.Eq("...with Retry-After: 60", "60", limited.Headers.TryGetValues("Retry-After", out var ra) ? ra.First() : null);
DojoWeb.Status($"GET /products #{i + 1} is not limited", 200, await http.GetAsync("/products"));

steps.title: Live lab: guess carol's password, then rate limit
prompt: In the **vulnerable shop** lab, do **Attack: guess a password** (hydra or a curl loop over `~/top-passwords.txt`) and **Fix: rate limit the sign-in** in `Auth.cs`. Then run hydra again and look at what it reports: tools need tuning against defences, and so do alerts.
steps.explain: After the fix, hydra misreads the 429 page as a success, because it has no failure text. The same lesson applies to your monitoring: count 429s, they are attack traffic.
